content: The portion size of a product consumed daily at a population level, along with its sodium content (e.g., salty condiments), can have a significant impact on public health. If available, data on the sales volume of products can help identify which items are most commonly consumed and would yield the greatest population-wide benefit if their sodium levels were reformulated or reduced. Setting sodium reduction targets for all products within a food category ensures a level playing field for all manufacturers, preventing any single manufacturer from being disadvantaged. This approach also ensures that the population benefits from reduced sodium intake, regardless of the specific products they purchase. To achieve this, countries should aim to collect sales volume data, if available, to identify commonly consumed products that would have the greatest population impact if sodium levels were reduced to target levels. The methodology for developing these benchmarks is detailed in the report, and the information used to create each of the regional benchmarks is provided in Supplementary File 1. Additional clarifications and methodological details have been included in the report in response to reviewer comments. Sodium ranges for product categories, at least as an annex, along with graphs or plots showing sodium levels of key products, would enable countries to adapt the benchmarks more easily. The report provides the distribution of sodium levels by presenting the 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile values. The 25th percentile represents the sodium content below which 25% of products fall, while the 75th percentile represents the sodium content below which 75% of products fall. This approach is considered more appropriate than providing the lowest and highest sodium levels in a category, as extreme values may result from labeling errors or unique products within the category. Countries are advised to use sodium content data from products available in their own food supply when adapting the regional benchmarks. This ensures that targets are set at levels appropriate for the specific country. Consequently, providing sodium content data plots from various South-East Asian countries in this report is not deemed beneficial for countries adapting these targets to their own contexts. To illustrate the use of frequency plots, an example of sodium levels for the nuts, seeds, and kernels category is included in the methodology section. In response to reviewer comments, the report has adopted the use of interquartile ranges instead of full ranges and has provided a set of summary statistics for each food category in Supplementary File 1. These statistics include the mean, median, 25th percentile, and 75th percentile values.
